title: German Arms Exports to Israel Surge on TKMS Submarine Deliveries as UK Rolls Out £416M Drone Overhaul
subhead: Germany approved close to €800 million in defense exports to Israel in the first half of 2026 — more than four times all of 2025 — centered on new submarine deliveries, while Britain finalized a £400 million drone contract to replace its Watchkeeper surveillance fleet.

sections.heading: German Arms Exports to Israel Nearly Quadruple on Submarine Program
sections.body: Berlin approved nearly €800 million ($930 million) in defense export licenses to Israel in the first half of 2026 — more than four times the total approved in all of 2025 — according to Der Spiegel, citing data from Germany's Ministry of Economics and Energy provided in response to a query from a leftist opposition party. The Anadolu Agency reported that export licenses surged to more than four times the amount approved in the previous year. Much of the surge is tied to the submarine program: Israeli media (Globes) note the INS Drakon, built by Germany's TKMS, is now en route to Israel. The Drakon is the largest submarine built in Germany since World War II, carrying a reported $634 million price tag (Fox News), and is seen as a major boost to Israel's second-strike deterrence posture against Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: The export numbers — driven by a flagship naval program rather than spare parts — show Germany's arms relationship with Israel continuing to expand at scale even as Berlin defends the policy before the ICJ. The Drakon's delivery simultaneously strengthens Israel's undersea deterrent during the ongoing Iran conflict.

sections.heading: British Army Replaces Watchkeeper With Ukraine-Proven Tekever AR5
sections.body: The UK Ministry of Defence confirmed it has formally awarded Portugal-based Tekever a contract worth up to £400 million ($530 million) to supply its twin-engine AR5 tactical surveillance drone, replacing the British Army's Thales Watchkeeper system in service since 2014 and withdrawn earlier this year (UK Defence Journal, Aviation Week). The deal begins with an initial order of six aircraft, rising to up to 24 by 2029, built at a new Tekever factory in Swindon. The AR5 — able to carry up to 50kg of sensors and already used by Ukraine against Russia — sits alongside a separate £16 million package delivering more than 1,000 small drones from three UK SMEs, including Evolve Dynamics' FOXE-NATO systems and 670 Skydio X10 INTL aircraft. Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard announced both at the Defence Vehicle Dynamics land warfare exhibition, framing them under Project Rapstone, which aims to double the Army's fighting power by 2027 and move new equipment to the front line within 24 months.
sections.whyItMatters: This is Britain's clearest signal yet that the Army's post-Strategic Defence Review force structure runs on uncrewed systems, and a case study in how battlefield experience in Ukraine is being converted directly into Western procurement — Tekever also expects to support more than 1,000 UK jobs by 2030.

sections.heading: UK Hands Ukraine Production Rights to Stone Cloak Electronic Warfare System
sections.body: London has transferred technology rights for its Stone Cloak electronic warfare system to Ukraine, allowing Kyiv to produce the system locally, according to multiple reports covering UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the Portsmouth naval base. Stone Cloak is a tablet-sized device designed to protect drones from detection and jamming, expanding Ukraine's capability to counter growing Russian unmanned operations. Burnham also pledged to share electronic warfare technology to protect Ukrainian drones as part of a broader support package.
sections.whyItMatters: Transferring production rights — rather than just units — is a qualitative step that shifts Ukraine toward self-reliance in electronic warfare as drone-on-drone attrition becomes central to the conflict, and reflects a trend of allies licensing systems rather than exporting finished hardware.

sections.heading: Houthi Drone and Missile Campaign Stretches Gulf Defenses and Energy Security
sections.body: Yemen's Houthis have escalated attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, and the Saudi-led coalition said on Sept. 19 its defenses intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile fired at Riyadh — the first alert sounded in the capital since the latest escalation (Al Jazeera). Saudi civil defense separately reported that falling debris from an intercepted Houthi drone killed one person and injured two (AP). Reports from NPR describe the Houthis' biggest land grab in years reigniting Yemen's civil war and pushing up global fuel prices, with the campaign threatening Saudi oil exports and the Bab El-Mandeb maritime chokepoint. Red Sea shipping has slowed as the attacks extend beyond Saudi installations.
sections.whyItMatters: The campaign tests Gulf integrated air and missile defense at civilian energy sites and a maritime chokepoint simultaneously — a pressure point that complicates the ongoing US-Iran diplomacy, since Houthi attacks are widely framed as aligned with Iranian-backed escalation across the region.

sections.heading: US-Iran Pause Exposes Depleted Precision-Missile Stocks
sections.body: As Washington pauses strikes on Iran for a third night to open space for Strait of Hormuz diplomacy, the military cost of the near-five-month war has come into focus. Reuters reported the US has used 'virtually all' of its long-range precision missiles — including ATACMS and PrSM — in the campaign, while the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated the war has cost around $2 billion per month and that replenishing depleted munitions stockpiles could take up to five years (congressional report via MSN). Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Gen. Dan Caine is reported to be privately pressing for an off-ramp, and President Trump has reportedly grown angry over public disclosures of the material strain, viewing them as weakening his negotiating position.
sections.whyItMatters: The munitions picture is now a central input into diplomacy: the pause reflects not just political will but finite precision-strike inventories. The multi-year replenishment timeline will shape US defense procurement priorities and industrial base investment well after any ceasefire.

sections.heading: India Warns Seafarers Black Sea Corridor 'Highly Volatile'
sections.body: India's Ministry of External Affairs has issued a fresh advisory warning Indian nationals to carefully assess risks before accepting jobs on commercial vessels operating in or transiting the Black Sea, citing the region as 'highly volatile' after a spate of drone and missile attacks by both Russia and Ukraine on shipping. The advisory follows deadly strikes off Ukraine and a surge in attacks on vessels in the corridor, and comes as a civilian grain ship sank after a Russian missile strike, according to regional coverage.
sections.whyItMatters: The advisory is a practical signal from a major maritime labor exporter that the Black Sea has become a high-risk war zone for civilian shipping — a factor that compounds insurance and re-routing pressures on grain and trade flows beyond the tactical battlefield.

bottomLine: Today's developments center on supply: Germany's arms exports to Israel nearly quadrupled in the first half of 2026, anchored by TKMS submarine deliveries that strengthen Israel's undersea deterrent, while Britain moved £416 million into uncrewed systems by replacing Watchkeeper with the Ukraine-proven Tekever AR5 and licensing its Stone Cloak electronic warfare technology to Ukraine. The Houthi drone-and-missile campaign against Saudi energy, India's Black Sea advisory, and disclosures that the US nearly exhausted ATACMS and PrSM stocks — with up to five years needed to replenish — all underline how the ongoing conflicts are reshaping procurement, industrial throughput, and force planning far beyond the front lines.
sources: UK Defence Journal, Aviation Week, Der Spiegel, Anadolu Agency, Globes, Fox News, Yahoo News, Al Jazeera, AP, NPR, Reuters, MSN, Congressional Budget Office report, India MEA advisory
